title: Demonstratives: hic, ille, iste, is, idem, ipse

objectives.can: Parse the demonstrative pronouns and tell their senses apart.

explanation.summary: Latin has no article, so it points with demonstratives: *hic* 'this', *ille* 'that', *iste* 'that of yours', *is* 'he, that', *idem* 'the same', *ipse* 'self'. They are very frequent, they change for case, number and gender, and in the Vulgate several of them begin to behave like the English 'he' and 'the'.

sections.heading: Six words, three jobs
body: A demonstrative can stand beside a noun (*hanc spem*, 'this hope') or stand alone as a pronoun (*ille*, 'that man, he'). In the library all six are filed as pronouns. The ones that point are *hic*, *ille* and *iste*; *is* is the weakest pointer and serves as the ordinary 'he, she, it' of the third person; *idem* adds 'the same'; and *ipse* stresses a noun or pronoun ('himself, the very one').

Grammarians traditionally tie the three pointers to the speaker: *hic* to what is near me, *iste* to what is near you (often with a tone of contempt or distance in classical prose), and *ille* to what is far from both, or well known. These are tendencies of classical Latin, and by the time of the Vulgate they are less firm.

sections.heading: The endings
body: The demonstratives decline like a pronoun, not like a noun. The mark of this declension is the genitive singular in -ius for every gender (*illius*, *istius*, *ipsius*, *eius*, *huius*) and the dative singular in -i (*huic*, *ei*). The nominative and accusative otherwise look like second-declension endings for masculine and neuter and first-declension endings for feminine, but with some irregular forms: neuter singular in -d (*illud*, *istud*, *id*), and a nominative masculine singular without -s in *ille*, *iste* and *ipse*. The table on this page shows the endings of *ille*.

*hic* has its own pattern: the stem is h- with the endings seen in *hunc*, *hanc*, *huic* and *huius*. *is* has the stem e- in most forms (*eum*, *eos*, *eorum*) and i- in some (*iis*). *idem* is *is* with the particle -dem added, and an m or n sits where they meet (*eumdem*, *eundem*; both spellings occur in the texts). *ipse* declines like *ille*, with *ipsum* in the neuter singular.

sections.heading: What the analysis can and cannot show
body: Many endings are shared between two cases or genders, and the analyser leaves such forms undecided. The dative singular, for instance, is -i in all genders (ill-i, ips-i), and the feminine nominative singular of *hic* and *ille* are written *haec* and *illa*. A form like *illis* can be dative or ablative plural, masculine, feminine or neuter. Only the clause decides, and where the analyser cannot decide a form, the questions do not use it.

sections.heading: Which to use for 'he'
body: Latin has no separate third-person pronoun. Where English says 'he saw him', Latin may use *is*, *ille* or only the verb ending. In the Vulgate *ille* is frequent as a plain 'he', in the nominative (*ille ambulavit*, 'he walked'), and *ipse* is frequently used for a person who is the centre of attention (*ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum*, 'it is he who will save his people').
The genitives *eius* and *eorum* are the ordinary words for 'his, her, its' and 'their' when the possessor is not the subject of the clause. They do not change to agree with the thing owned.

sections.heading: idem and ipse
body: *idem* means 'the same' and agrees with its noun: *eumdem sermonem*, 'the same word'. *ipse* does not mean 'the same'. It intensifies: *in ipso manere* is 'to abide in him himself'. It is also used to say that the thing itself, and not another, is meant, and in the Vulgate, like *ille*, it can be as weak as 'he'.

misunderstandings: *ipse* does not mean 'the same'; that is *idem*. The two are often mixed up because they begin alike in some English glosses ('the same self').
*is* is not the verb 'to be'. *id* and *is* are forms of a pronoun; the verb has *est*, *sunt*, *esse*.
*eius* does not agree with the noun it goes with. In *nomen eius* the word *eius* is genitive singular of *is* and means 'his, her' whatever the gender of the name.
*illis*, *eis* and *ipsis* are not one case: the same ending serves the dative and the ablative plural, so a form like *illis* needs the clause to decide.

deeper.heading: Weakening of ille and ipse
body: In the speech from which French, Italian and Spanish descend, *ille* became the definite article, and *ipse* gave some Romance forms of 'same' and the article. The Vulgate, translating Greek, stands on the way: *ille* often stands where the Greek has a plain 'he' or the article, and *ipse* is sometimes simply 'he'. Plater and White note this in their grammar of the Vulgate. When you read a late text, ask whether the word is pointing, or only standing for 'he'.

paradigms.title: The endings of ille
paradigms.caption: The stem is ill-. Iste and ipse have the same endings on the stems ist- and ips-, except that ipse has -um in the neuter singular.

paradigms.note: The dative and ablative plural are the same form, and so are the nominative and accusative of the neuter. The forms are shown by their endings because the analysed texts leave many of them undecided.

examples.analysis: *hunc* is the accusative singular masculine of *hic*, 'this', agreeing with *mundum* after *in*: 'into this world'. It is the nearest-pointing demonstrative, and here it points to the world of the speaker.

quoted.title: 1 John
quoted.english: He that saith he abideth in him, ought himself also to walk, even as he walked.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: Three pronouns in one verse. *ipso* is the ablative of *ipse*, 'in him'; *ille* is nominative singular masculine, 'he', and is the subject of *ambulavit*; and *ipse* in the nominative says 'he himself ought to walk'. The two words are not interchangeable: *ille* names the one who walked, *ipse* puts the weight on the person who must do the same.

options: It stresses the subject: 'he too, himself'
It means 'the same man' and so refers to someone else
It points to something near the speaker
check.explain: *ipse* is the emphatic pronoun: it puts weight on the person who must act. It does not point (*hic*, *ille*) and it is not *idem*, 'the same'.

options: As 'he', the subject of the clause, with little pointing force
